To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dietary omega 3 PUFAs can be incorporated into eggs, but the deposition is limited by the amount of omega 3s supplied in the diet and by the hen's ability to synthesize omega 3 LC-PUFA.

the inclusion of either flax seed oil or DHA in the feed of hens results in a linear increase in the omega 3 fatty acid content of the egg yolk.
dietary omega 3 LC-PUFA (ALA or DHA) can be effectively utilized by laying hens for the production of omega 3 LC PUFA enriched eggs, with DHA showing superior deposition efficiency compared to ALA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach to enrich eggs with omega 3 PUFAs.
the identification of the underlying regulatory mechanisms of the deposition of omega 3 PU FA in eggs.
the impact of graded level of omega 3 PUFAs (ALA and DHA) on egg production performance, egg quality and plasma lipids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the deposition of DHA in the egg yolk is dependent on the amount of DHA consumed by hens and that the endogenous synthesis of LCPUFA is not a major contributor to the DHA content of the egg.
the incorporation of omega 2 LCPUFA in the egg is a dynamic process, which is dependent on the dietary source of omega 2 PUFA and the level of intake.
the inclusion of omega 3 PUFAs in laying hen diets is a feasible approach to increase the omega 3 PU FA content of the egg yolk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
both exogenous and endogenous synthesis of n-3 LCPUFA are subject to a similar mechanism of regulation.

the incorporation of omega 6 and omega 3 LC PUFA in the egg is regulated by the availability and metabolism of the respective precursor fatty acids in the liver and the subsequent transfer efficiency to the egg.
both ALA and DHA can be utilized for the production of DHA in the eggs.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the incorporation of omega 6 PUFA in the egg was not affected by the dietary omega 3 PUFAs and that the dietary inclusion levels of total omega 6 and omega 3 PUFs were not associated with changes in plasma cholesterol and eggshell quality.
the incorporation of omega 6 PUFA in eggs is not affected by dietary omega 6 PUFAs.
the inclusion of 0.60 % total omega 3 PUFAs in the background diet is required to achieve maximal enrichment of DHA in eggs.
